lessons.title: Collect structured choices with select, textarea and button
lessons.summary: Build drop-down menus with select, option and optgroup, capture free text with textarea, and understand the three button types.
lessons.goal: Assemble a support-request form that uses a grouped drop-down, a multi-line text field and a real submit button.
lessons.whyItMatters: Almost every real form needs more than single-line text boxes: users pick a category, write a longer message, and press a button that actually submits. The select, textarea and button elements are the workhorses behind those interactions, and each has quirks — like textarea storing its default text as content instead of a value attribute — that regularly trip up developers. Knowing them cold means your forms submit exactly the data you expect.
steps: Read the theory on select and option first — pay attention to which part of an option is submitted.
Add the department drop-down with named options (tasks 1 and 2).
Preselect the most common choice with the selected attribute (task 3).
Group the options into two labelled optgroups (task 4).
Build the message textarea with rows, cols and default content (task 5).
Finish with a real submit button and run all checks (task 6).
lessons.prompt:
<select name="department">
  <optgroup label="Technical">
    <option value="bug" selected>Bug report</option>
    <option value="outage">Service outage</option>
  </optgroup>
  <optgroup label="Account">
    <option value="billing">Billing</option>
    <option value="access">Access request</option>
  </optgroup>
</select>
<textarea name="message" rows="4" cols="40">Describe your issue here.</textarea>
<button type="submit">Send request</button>
lessons.explanation: The select carries the name, so the form submits one pair like department=bug. Each option keeps a short machine-friendly value while showing human-friendly text, and selected marks the default choice. The optgroup labels organise a long list without becoming selectable themselves. The textarea's default text sits between its tags — it has no value attribute — and the button declares type="submit" explicitly so its behaviour never depends on browser defaults.
lessons.example:
A helpdesk form that asks users to type the department name by hand receives 'billing', 'Billing dept', 'bills' and countless typos, which no backend can route reliably.

Replace it with a select whose options carry fixed values (bug, outage, billing, access) grouped under Technical and Account headings: every submission now contains one of four known strings, the default case is preselected, and a textarea gives users room to explain the problem in their own words.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, complete the support-request form: add a department select with four valued options, preselect one, organise them into two optgroups, add a message textarea with rows, cols and default text, and finish with an explicit submit button.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a drop-down with two grouped sections of options (one already chosen), a multi-line text box containing starter text, and a Send request button. All six checks pass.
commonMistakes: Putting the name attribute on option instead of select. The select owns the name; each option only supplies a value.
Writing <textarea value="..."> to set default text. Textarea ignores a value attribute — its default content goes between the opening and closing tags.
Forgetting type on button. Inside a form, a bare <button> defaults to type="submit", so a button you meant as a helper accidentally submits the form.
Making optgroup labels do the work of a first option. An optgroup label cannot be selected — if you need a 'please choose' entry, add a real option with an empty value.
lessons.proTip: Leave the textarea's tags on the same line when it should start empty: any whitespace or line break between <textarea> and </textarea> becomes real default content, and users end up submitting invisible newlines.

coding.intro: You will build the input side of a support-request form: a grouped drop-down, a multi-line message box and a proper submit button.

sections.heading: select and option: a drop-down with a contract
sections.body:
A select element renders as a drop-down list. Its children are option elements, one per choice. Two attributes make the pair useful: name on the select and value on each option. When the form submits, the browser sends one name/value pair — the select's name combined with the value of whichever option the user picked.

The text between an option's tags is what the user sees; the value attribute is what the server receives. Keeping them separate is the whole point: the visible label can say 'Bug report — something is broken' while the submitted value stays a clean machine token like bug. If you omit value entirely, the browser falls back to submitting the option's visible text, which couples your backend to your on-screen wording — rename a label and you silently change your data.

A select always submits something (the first option, if the user never touches it), so the classic 'please choose' prompt is written as a real option with an empty value. Combined with the required attribute on the select, an empty value blocks submission until the user makes an actual choice.
sections.code:
<label for="dept">Department</label>
<select id="dept" name="department">
  <option value="">-- Please choose --</option>
  <option value="bug">Bug report</option>
  <option value="billing">Billing question</option>
</select>

sections.heading: Preselecting with the selected attribute
sections.body:
By default the first option in the list is shown when the page loads. To start on a different choice, add the boolean selected attribute to exactly one option. Boolean means its presence alone activates it — <option selected> and <option selected="selected"> behave identically, and there is no way to write it as 'false'.

Preselecting is a design decision, not just a convenience. If eighty percent of tickets are bug reports, preselecting bug saves most users a click. But a preselected option also means users can submit without ever looking at the field — never preselect anything with legal or financial consequences, such as an opt-in to marketing email.

If you accidentally mark several options selected in a single-choice select, the browser keeps only the last one. In a multiple select (covered below), several selected attributes are legitimate and all of them start highlighted.
sections.code:
<select name="priority">
  <option value="low">Low</option>
  <option value="normal" selected>Normal</option>
  <option value="high">High</option>
</select>

sections.heading: Organising long lists with optgroup
sections.body:
Once a drop-down grows past a handful of entries, users start scanning instead of reading. The optgroup element groups related options under a bold, non-selectable heading supplied by its label attribute. The browser indents the options beneath each heading, so a thirty-item list reads as three or four short lists.

An optgroup is purely structural: it never submits anything and cannot be picked. Its label attribute is required in practice — a group without a label renders as an unlabelled gap and tells the user nothing. Options that belong to no group can sit directly inside the select alongside groups, before or after them.

Screen readers announce the group label when the user enters a group, so optgroup is also an accessibility win: 'Technical, group, Bug report' is far clearer than a flat wall of thirty options.
sections.code:
<select name="department">
  <optgroup label="Technical">
    <option value="bug">Bug report</option>
    <option value="outage">Service outage</option>
  </optgroup>
  <optgroup label="Account">
    <option value="billing">Billing</option>
    <option value="access">Access request</option>
  </optgroup>
</select>

sections.heading: size and multiple: from drop-down to list box
sections.body:
Two attributes change how a select looks and behaves. The size attribute sets how many rows are visible at once: size="1" is the familiar drop-down, while size="5" turns the control into an always-open scrolling list box five rows tall. No options are hidden either way — size only controls the viewport.

The boolean multiple attribute allows the user to pick more than one option, using Ctrl-click (Cmd-click on macOS) or Shift-click for ranges. Browsers render a multiple select as an open list box automatically, because a closed drop-down cannot show several highlighted rows at once. On submission, the browser sends one name/value pair per selected option, so the server receives the same name repeated — backends must be written to expect a list, not a single string.

Be honest about the usability cost: many users do not know the Ctrl-click convention, and on touch screens it barely works. For most multi-choice interfaces a group of checkboxes is friendlier; reserve select multiple for dense administrative screens where space is tight.
sections.code:
<select name="affected" multiple size="4">
  <option value="web">Web app</option>
  <option value="api">API</option>
  <option value="mobile">Mobile app</option>
  <option value="email">Email delivery</option>
</select>

sections.heading: textarea: multi-line text with content, not value
sections.body:
The textarea element captures multi-line free text: bug descriptions, comments, cover letters. Unlike input, it is not self-closing and — crucially — it has no value attribute. Its default text is whatever sits between <textarea> and </textarea>. Writing value="..." on a textarea does nothing; the attribute is silently ignored. This is the single most common textarea mistake.

The rows and cols attributes set the initial visible size: rows counts lines of text, cols counts average character widths. They shape the starting box only — users can usually drag-resize it, and CSS width/height override both. Still, supplying sensible rows and cols means the control is usable even before any stylesheet loads.

The wrap attribute controls how line breaks are submitted. With the default wrap="soft", text visually wraps in the box but the submitted value contains only the line breaks the user actually typed. With wrap="hard" (which requires cols to be set), the browser inserts a real newline at every visual wrap point before submitting — useful for systems that expect fixed-width text, and surprising everywhere else. Like every form control, a textarea needs a name to be submitted and a label for accessibility.
sections.code:
<label for="msg">Describe the problem</label>
<textarea id="msg" name="message" rows="6" cols="50" wrap="soft">Describe your issue here.</textarea>

sections.heading: The button element and its three types
sections.body:
The button element creates a clickable control, and its type attribute decides what clicking does. type="submit" sends the surrounding form to the server. type="reset" restores every control in the form to its initial value — a feature users hit by accident far more often than on purpose, so use it rarely. type="button" does nothing on its own; it exists purely as a hook for JavaScript.

Here is the trap: inside a form, a button with no type attribute behaves as type="submit". Add an innocent 'Show password' helper button without a type, and every click submits the half-finished form. Professional habit: always write the type explicitly on every button.

What makes button better than the older <input type="submit">? Content freedom. An input renders only the plain text of its value attribute, while a button is a container: it can hold formatted text, an icon image, an svg, or any combination. That flexibility is why modern interfaces are built almost exclusively with the button element.

lessons.title: Fine-tune every input with the full attribute toolkit
lessons.summary: Control defaults, hints, editability, length, numeric ranges, focus, autofill and mobile keyboards with the input element's attribute set.
lessons.goal: Configure a checkout-style form where every input uses the right combination of value, placeholder, constraints, autocomplete and inputmode.
lessons.whyItMatters: The input element is one tag with dozens of behaviours, and the attributes are where the real control lives. The difference between readonly and disabled decides whether data reaches your server; autocomplete tokens decide whether browsers can autofill a checkout in two seconds or force users to type everything; inputmode decides which keyboard a phone shows. Forms built with the right attributes convert measurably better and generate cleaner data.
steps: Read the theory sections in order — the readonly vs disabled distinction is the most important.
Add a placeholder hint to the search field (task 1).
Lock the account ID as readonly with a prefilled value (task 2).
Constrain the quantity field with min, max and step (task 3).
Cap the username length with maxlength (task 4).
Wire up autocomplete on the email field and a numeric keyboard for the code field (tasks 5 and 6), then run the checks.
lessons.prompt:
<input type="text" name="account" value="AC-10442" readonly>
<input type="number" name="qty" min="1" max="10" step="1" value="1">
<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" placeholder="you@example.com">
<input type="text" name="otp" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="one-time-code" maxlength="6">
lessons.explanation: The readonly account field shows a prefilled value the user cannot edit but that still submits with the form. The number input constrains quantity to whole numbers from 1 to 10, enforced by the spinner and by validation. The email field's autocomplete token lets the browser fill a saved address instantly, and the one-time-code field asks phones for a digits-only keyboard with inputmode while capping input at six characters.
lessons.example:
A checkout form with bare <input type="text"> fields makes users type their email on a full letter keyboard, lets them order -3 items, and loses the account number when someone edits it by accident.

The same form with attributes applied: the account ID is visible but locked, quantity is clamped to a sane range, email autofills from the browser's saved profile, and the SMS code field pops a large numeric keypad on phones. Nothing changed on the server — every improvement came from attributes.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, upgrade the plain order form: add a placeholder, a readonly prefilled field, numeric range constraints, a length cap, an autocomplete token and a numeric inputmode.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a form where the account ID cannot be edited, quantity uses spinner arrows within 1–10, and hint text appears in the empty search box. All six checks pass.
commonMistakes: Using disabled when you meant readonly. A disabled control is skipped at submission, so the server never receives its value; readonly submits normally.
Treating placeholder as a label. Placeholder text vanishes the moment typing starts — every field still needs a real <label>.
Confusing size with maxlength. size only widens the visible box; it does not stop the user typing more characters.
Writing autocomplete="false". The valid off switch is autocomplete="off", and even that is a hint browsers may overrule for saved logins.
lessons.proTip: When you want a numeric keypad but the value is not really a number — card numbers, postal codes, one-time codes — use type="text" with inputmode="numeric" instead of type="number". You keep leading zeros and avoid the spinner arrows.

coding.intro: You will take a bare order form and apply the attributes that control defaults, editability, length, ranges, autofill and mobile keyboards.

sections.heading: value and placeholder: defaults versus hints
sections.body:
The value attribute sets an input's initial content — real data that sits in the field on page load, can be edited, and is submitted with the form. Use it to prefill known information: a saved shipping city, a suggested quantity of 1, the user's current display name on a settings page.

The placeholder attribute is entirely different: pale hint text shown only while the field is empty. It never submits, and it disappears the instant the user types. Its job is to show an example of the expected format, like you@example.com or DD/MM/YYYY.

A placeholder must never replace a label. Because the hint vanishes during typing, users who get interrupted return to a form full of anonymous boxes and cannot remember what each one wanted. Screen readers also treat placeholders inconsistently. The reliable pattern is both: a visible label naming the field, plus an optional placeholder demonstrating the format.
sections.code:
<label for="city">City</label>
<input type="text" id="city" name="city" value="Athens">

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

sections.heading: readonly versus disabled: the submission difference
sections.body:
Both attributes stop the user editing a field, and that surface similarity hides a critical difference. A readonly input cannot be typed into, but it is still a live part of the form: it can be focused, its text can be selected and copied, and — the key point — its value IS submitted to the server.

A disabled input is switched off entirely: greyed out, unfocusable, unclickable, and excluded from submission. When the form serialises, a disabled field simply does not exist. If your server expects that field's name, it receives nothing.

Choose by intent. Readonly says 'this is confirmed data you may see but not change' — an order number, a locked username, a calculated total that must still reach the server. Disabled says 'this option does not currently apply' — a shipping-speed choice that is impossible for the selected country. Disabled also works on button, select and textarea, and on a whole fieldset to switch off an entire section at once.
sections.code:
<!-- Submits value AC-10442 -->
<input type="text" name="account" value="AC-10442" readonly>

<!-- Submits nothing at all -->
<input type="text" name="coupon" value="EXPIRED" disabled>

sections.heading: size versus maxlength and minlength
sections.body:
Three attributes deal with length, and only two of them limit anything. The size attribute is purely visual: size="30" makes the box wide enough for roughly thirty average characters, but the user can keep typing past it and the text scrolls. In modern work CSS usually controls width, so size is mostly seen in legacy code.

maxlength is a hard input cap: with maxlength="12" the browser refuses to accept a thirteenth character, whether typed or pasted. It is the right tool when a backend column or protocol has a fixed limit, such as a 12-character username or a 6-digit code.

minlength sets the shortest acceptable entry, but works differently: it cannot stop short input from being typed — it flags the field invalid at submission time instead, blocking submit until the text reaches the minimum. Note that minlength only fires once the user has entered something; an empty non-required field passes. Pair it with required when a value must exist and be long enough.
sections.code:
<label for="user">Username (3-12 chars)</label>
<input type="text" id="user" name="username"
       minlength="3" maxlength="12" size="15">

sections.heading: min, max and step for numeric and date inputs
sections.body:
Inputs that carry ordered values — number, range, date, time, month, week and the datetime types — accept three constraint attributes. min and max define the allowed interval: a quantity from 1 to 10, a birth date no later than today, an appointment no earlier than tomorrow. The spinner arrows and pickers respect the bounds, and typed values outside them make the field invalid at submit time.

step sets the spacing between allowed values, counted from min (or from zero if min is absent). step="1" means whole numbers; step="0.5" allows halves; on a date input step counts days. A value that does not land on the grid is invalid — with min="0" and step="5", the value 7 is rejected. If you genuinely want any decimal, write step="any".

These constraints double as documentation: a colleague reading min="1" max="10" step="1" knows the business rule without opening the backend. But remember they run in the user's browser and are trivially bypassed — the server must re-check every bound.
sections.code:
<label for="qty">Quantity</label>
<input type="number" id="qty" name="qty" min="1" max="10" step="1" value="1">

<label for="rating">Rating</label>
<input type="range" id="rating" name="rating" min="0" max="5" step="0.5">

sections.heading: multiple and autofocus
sections.body:
The boolean multiple attribute lets one input hold several values, and it applies to exactly two types. On type="email" it accepts a comma-separated list of addresses, each validated individually. On type="file" it lets the user pick several files in one dialog. On any other input type it does nothing.

autofocus, also boolean, moves keyboard focus into a control as soon as the page loads, so the user can start typing immediately — the classic example is a search page whose whole purpose is one field. Only one element per page may carry it; if several do, the first one wins.

Use autofocus sparingly. Jumping focus scrolls the page to the control and, for screen-reader users, skips them past everything above it — headings, instructions, error summaries. It belongs on pages with a single dominant task, never on the third field of a long form.
sections.code:
<input type="search" name="q" autofocus placeholder="Search products">
<input type="email" name="cc" multiple placeholder="a@x.com, b@y.com">

sections.heading: autocomplete: off, on, and the field tokens
sections.body:
The autocomplete attribute tells the browser what a field contains so it can offer saved data. autocomplete="on" (the default in most cases) lets the browser guess; autocomplete="off" asks it not to autofill — a request browsers honour unevenly, and often ignore for login fields because password managers deliberately override it.

The real power is the token vocabulary. Standardised values name the data precisely: name, given-name, family-name, email, tel, organization, street-address, address-line1, postal-code, country, bday, cc-number, cc-exp, new-password, current-password and one-time-code, among others. A checkout marked up with the right tokens autofills completely in one click, on every major browser, from data the user already saved.

Two tokens deserve special mention. new-password on a registration form tells password managers to offer a generated password instead of filling the old one. one-time-code on an SMS-verification field lets mobile browsers read the incoming code and suggest it above the keyboard — turning a copy-and-paste chore into a single tap.
sections.code:
<input type="text" name="fullname" autocomplete="name">
<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">
<input type="password" name="pw" autocomplete="new-password">
<input type="text" name="otp" autocomplete="one-time-code">

sections.heading: spellcheck and inputmode
sections.body:
spellcheck controls the red squiggly underline. It takes explicit values — spellcheck="true" or spellcheck="false" — and matters most where checking is noise: usernames, code snippets, product SKUs, email addresses. Browsers decide the default per element, so set it explicitly when you care either way.

inputmode does not validate anything; it chooses which virtual keyboard touch devices show. Its values: none (no keyboard — the page supplies its own widget), text (standard layout), numeric (digits 0-9), decimal (digits plus the decimal separator), tel (phone keypad with * and #), email (letters plus @ and .), url (with / and .com), and search (Enter key relabelled Search).

inputmode pairs naturally with type="text": a card-number field wants a digit keypad but must keep leading zeros and spaces that type="number" would destroy. Desktop browsers ignore inputmode completely — it costs nothing there and dramatically improves phone ergonomics, which is where most form abandonment happens.
sections.code:
<input type="text" name="card" inputmode="numeric" spellcheck="false"
       autocomplete="cc-number" placeholder="1234 5678 9012 3456">

lessons.title: Validate form input in the browser before it ever leaves the page
lessons.summary: Use required, pattern, length and range constraints plus type-driven checks to catch bad input instantly — and learn when to switch validation off.
lessons.goal: Add complete client-side validation to a sign-up form: required fields, a regex pattern with a helpful hint, length and range limits, and a draft button that bypasses it all.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every round-trip to the server for a missing email address wastes seconds and frustrates users. HTML's built-in validation catches empty fields, malformed addresses and out-of-range numbers before submission, with zero JavaScript. Just as importantly, knowing its limits — and why the server must always re-validate — separates developers who build secure forms from those who build breachable ones.
steps: Read how required and type-driven validation work, then look at the starter sign-up form.
Mark the username and email fields required (task 1).
Switch the email field to the validating email type (task 2).
Add a pattern with a title hint to the invite code (task 3).
Enforce a minimum password length (task 4) and an age range (task 5).
Add a Save draft button that skips validation with formnovalidate (task 6), then run the checks.
lessons.prompt:
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <input type="text" name="username" required minlength="3">
  <input type="email" name="email" required>
  <input type="text" name="invite" pattern="[A-Z]{3}-[0-9]{4}"
         title="Three capital letters, a dash, four digits, e.g. ABC-1234">
  <input type="password" name="pw" minlength="8" required>
  <input type="number" name="age" min="18" max="120">
  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
  <button type="submit" formnovalidate>Save draft</button>
</form>
lessons.explanation: Each constraint lives on the field it protects: required blocks empty submission, type="email" checks the address shape, pattern enforces a custom invite-code format with title supplying the human explanation shown in the error bubble, minlength guards the password, and min/max bound the age. The Save draft button carries formnovalidate, so incomplete drafts can still be stored — validation is per-submission, not per-form, when you need it to be.
lessons.example:
Without validation, a sign-up form happily posts an empty username, 'asdf' as an email and an age of -5; the server rejects it, the page reloads, and the user starts over.

With the constraints in place, the browser blocks submission instantly, focuses the first broken field, and shows a message next to it — 'Please fill in this field', or the pattern's title text for the invite code. The user fixes everything in one pass without a single network request.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, harden the sign-up form: required fields, a validating email type, a pattern with title on the invite code, a minimum password length, an age range, and a draft button that bypasses the checks.
lessons.expectedResult: Submitting the empty form in the preview triggers browser error bubbles instead of a submission; the Save draft button submits regardless. All six checks pass.
commonMistakes: Trusting client-side validation as security. Anyone can bypass it with DevTools or curl — the server must re-validate everything, always.
Writing a pattern without a title. The browser's default error ('Please match the requested format') tells users nothing about what the format actually is.
Wrapping the pattern in slashes or anchors like /^...$/. HTML patterns are automatically anchored to the whole value; write just the expression body.
Adding required to a radio group's every button but forgetting it works per-group: one required on any radio in the group makes the whole group mandatory.
lessons.proTip: Style broken fields live with the :invalid and :valid CSS pseudo-classes — for example input:invalid { border-color: #c00; }. Consider :user-invalid where supported, which waits until the user has actually interacted with the field instead of marking a pristine form red.

coding.intro: You will equip a sign-up form with the complete built-in validation toolkit, then deliberately punch one hole in it for saving drafts.

sections.heading: How built-in validation works
sections.body:
When a form is submitted, the browser first walks every control and checks its constraints. If any control fails, submission stops: nothing is sent, the first invalid field receives focus, and a message bubble explains the problem. All of this ships with the browser — no JavaScript, no library.

Constraints come from attributes you already know as data hints: required, pattern, minlength, maxlength, min, max, step, and the input type itself. Validation only runs at submission (and for some checks while typing), so users are never interrupted mid-thought with premature errors.

The browser also reflects validity into CSS: at any moment every control matches either the :valid or :invalid pseudo-class, which lets a stylesheet tint broken fields red or valid ones green without any script. That is the entire styling hook in one sentence — the logic stays in HTML, the paint job in CSS.
sections.code:
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="u">Username</label>
  <input type="text" id="u" name="username" required>
  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>

sections.heading: required: the non-negotiable fields
sections.body:
The boolean required attribute marks a control that must hold a value before the form can submit. On text-like inputs it rejects the empty string; on a checkbox it demands the box be ticked (the classic terms-and-conditions pattern); on a select it rejects an option whose value is empty, which is why placeholder options are written as <option value="">.

For radio buttons, required is evaluated per group: putting it on any one button of a name-sharing group makes the whole group mandatory — the user must pick some option, not that specific one.

Mark fields required deliberately, not defensively. Every mandatory field measurably increases abandonment, so a good form demands only what the process genuinely needs and labels the rest optional.
sections.code:
<input type="checkbox" id="terms" name="terms" required>
<label for="terms">I accept the terms</label>

<select name="country" required>
  <option value="">-- Choose a country --</option>
  <option value="gr">Greece</option>
</select>

sections.heading: Type-driven validation: email and url
sections.body:
Some input types are constraints in themselves. type="email" requires the value to look like an address: something, an @ sign, and a domain part. type="url" requires an absolute URL including its scheme — https://example.com passes, example.com alone does not, which surprises users often enough that many sites pre-fill or auto-repair the scheme.

Be clear about what email validation does and does not promise. It checks shape, not existence: a@b passes the browser check even though it points nowhere. Verifying that an address is real and owned by the user requires a server-side confirmation email — the browser can only stop obvious typos.

These types stack with other attributes: type="email" required multiple validates a mandatory, comma-separated list of addresses, each checked individually.
sections.code:
<input type="email" name="email" required>
<input type="url" name="website" placeholder="https://example.com">

sections.heading: pattern and title: custom formats with human hints
sections.body:
When no input type matches your format, the pattern attribute accepts a regular expression that the entire value must match. The expression is implicitly anchored — the browser wraps it as ^(?:pattern)$ — so pattern="[A-Z]{3}-[0-9]{4}" means the whole value is exactly three capitals, a dash, four digits. Do not add slashes or ^...$ yourself.

A pattern without explanation produces the least helpful error on the web: 'Please match the requested format.' The title attribute fixes this — its text is appended to the browser's error bubble, so title="Three capital letters, a dash, four digits, e.g. ABC-1234" turns a dead end into an instruction. Treat pattern and title as a mandatory pair.

An empty value passes a pattern check: pattern constrains what a value looks like if present, while required makes it present. Format-critical mandatory fields need both. Pattern applies to text, search, tel, url, email and password inputs — not to number, where min/max/step do the work.
sections.code:
<label for="invite">Invite code</label>
<input type="text" id="invite" name="invite" required
       pattern="[A-Z]{3}-[0-9]{4}"
       title="Three capital letters, a dash, four digits, e.g. ABC-1234">

sections.heading: Length and range constraints at validation time
sections.body:
minlength and maxlength bound the character count. They behave asymmetrically: maxlength prevents over-typing outright, while minlength lets the user type freely and flags the field invalid at submission if the text is present but too short. A password field with minlength="8" is the canonical use.

min, max and step validate ordered types — number, range, date, time and friends. A typed value below min or above max fails; so does a value that misses the step grid counted from min. Date inputs accept ISO strings for their bounds: min="2026-01-01" refuses any earlier date, and the picker greys those days out.

All length and range failures produce specific browser messages ('Value must be greater than or equal to 1'), localised to the user's language automatically — one more thing you do not have to build.
sections.code:
<input type="password" name="pw" minlength="8" required>
<input type="number" name="age" min="18" max="120">
<input type="date" name="start" min="2026-01-01">

sections.heading: Switching validation off: novalidate and formnovalidate
sections.body:
Sometimes you need a form to submit despite broken constraints. The novalidate attribute on the form element disables built-in validation for every submission of that form — common when a site replaces browser bubbles with its own JavaScript validation UI but keeps the attributes for semantics.

The finer tool is formnovalidate on a specific submit button: only submissions triggered by that button skip validation, while every other button still enforces it. The textbook case is Save draft next to Publish — a half-finished draft should be storable even though the title field is still empty.

formnovalidate belongs on submit buttons (button or input type="submit") and is one of a family of form* button attributes (formaction, formmethod) that override the parent form's settings per button.
sections.code:
<form action="/articles" method="post">
  <input type="text" name="title" required>
  <button type="submit">Publish</button>
  <button type="submit" formnovalidate>Save draft</button>
</form>

sections.heading: Why the server must validate anyway
sections.body:
Client-side validation is a user-experience feature, not a security boundary. Every check described here runs in software the user fully controls: opening DevTools and deleting a required attribute takes five seconds, and tools like curl skip the browser entirely, posting whatever bytes an attacker likes straight to your endpoint.

So the rule is absolute: the server re-validates everything — presence, type, length, range, format, and business rules the browser cannot know, like whether the username is already taken. Client-side validation exists to catch honest mistakes instantly and cut server round-trips; server-side validation exists to protect your data. You always need both, and they should enforce the same rules so honest users never see a server rejection the browser missed.

lessons.title: Suggest, calculate and measure with datalist, output, meter and progress
lessons.summary: Give text fields autocomplete suggestions with datalist, show calculated results with output, and pick correctly between the meter gauge and the progress bar.
lessons.goal: Build a system-status panel that combines a suggesting input, a live-result output, a disk-usage meter and a backup progress bar.
lessons.whyItMatters: These four elements replace common JavaScript widgets with native HTML: datalist gives you autocomplete without a library, output marks calculation results so assistive tech announces them, and meter and progress render accessible gauges and bars styled by the operating system. Knowing the semantic line between meter (a measurement within known bounds) and progress (task completion) keeps your interfaces meaningful to screen readers, not just visually plausible.
steps: Read how datalist differs from select — suggestions versus a closed list.
Create the datalist of server names and connect it to the input with the list attribute (tasks 1-3).
Add an output element wired to its source fields with the for attribute (task 4).

<input list="servers" name="server">
<datalist id="servers">
  <option value="web-01">
  <option value="web-02">
  <option value="db-01">
</datalist>

<output name="result" for="a b">42</output>
<meter value="0.72" min="0" max="1" low="0.25" high="0.75" optimum="0.1">72%</meter>
<progress value="30" max="100">30%</progress>
lessons.explanation: The input's list attribute points at the datalist's id, turning a free-text field into one with drop-down suggestions the user may ignore. The output element declares 'this is a result computed from the fields named in for'. The meter shows a scalar measurement — 72% disk usage — with low/high/optimum telling the browser which zones are good (it recolours the bar accordingly), while progress reports how much of a running task is done.
lessons.example:
A deployment form with a plain text field forces operators to remember exact server names; a select would block the new server added yesterday.

A datalist gives the best of both: typing 'we' suggests web-01 and web-02, but typing a brand-new name still works. Next to it, a meter shows the chosen server's disk at 72% — amber, because usage crossed the high mark — and a progress bar tracks the backup that is 30% complete.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that datalist offers suggestions, not restrictions — users can type anything. If only listed values are valid, validate with pattern or server-side, or use a select.
Mismatching the input's list attribute and the datalist's id. The connection is by exact id; a typo silently disables all suggestions.
Using meter for task completion or progress for a measurement. Meter answers 'how full/high is this value?', progress answers 'how much of the work is done?'.
Omitting max on progress and wondering why value="30" renders full — without max the scale defaults to 1.0, so any value of 1 or more reads as complete.
lessons.proTip: A progress element with no value attribute at all renders as an indeterminate animated bar — the correct way to say 'working, duration unknown'. Add the value later from JavaScript when you can measure real progress.

sections.heading: datalist: suggestions, not a closed list
sections.body:
A datalist holds a set of option elements that a browser offers as autocomplete suggestions for a text-like input. The wiring has two ends: the datalist gets an id, and the input gets a list attribute whose value is that exact id. When the user focuses the input or starts typing, matching options drop down; picking one fills the field.

The crucial contrast with select: a select is a closed vocabulary — the user must pick a listed option — while a datalist is advisory. The user can accept a suggestion, or type something entirely absent from the list, and both submit fine. That makes datalist ideal for 'common answers plus free text' fields: departure cities, tags, server names, job titles.

Options inside a datalist are usually written as void-style tags with only a value attribute: <option value="web-01">. They can carry label text too, which some browsers show as a secondary line. The datalist itself renders nothing — it can sit anywhere in the body, and one datalist can serve several inputs. The list attribute also works with some non-text types: range inputs use it to draw tick marks, and color inputs to offer swatches.
sections.code:
<label for="server">Target server</label>
<input type="text" id="server" name="server" list="servers">
<datalist id="servers">
  <option value="web-01">
  <option value="web-02">
  <option value="db-01">
  <option value="cache-01">
</datalist>

sections.heading: When to choose datalist versus select
sections.body:
Choose by asking one question: is the answer space closed or open? Shipping country is closed — you deliver to a fixed set, so a select guarantees valid data. Job title is open — no list covers every title, so a datalist accelerates common cases without blocking rare ones.

Remember that a datalist provides zero validation. If a user types 'web-99' into the server field and that server does not exist, the form still submits it. When listed values are strongly preferred but not absolutely required, pair the datalist with server-side handling of unknowns; when they are required, either add a pattern or switch to a select.

One practical caveat: suggestion UI varies noticeably between browsers — how many options show, how matching works (prefix versus substring) — so treat datalist as progressive enhancement, never as a load-bearing part of your layout.

sections.heading: output: a labelled home for results
sections.body:
The output element marks text that is the result of a calculation or user action: an order total, a converted currency amount, the value a range slider currently points at. Visually it is unremarkable inline text; semantically it tells the browser 'this region shows computed results'.

Two attributes matter. name makes the output addressable through the form like any control (though outputs are not submitted — they are display, not input). The for attribute lists the ids of the fields the result was computed from, space-separated, documenting the data flow: for="price qty" says this number derives from those two inputs.

The accessibility payoff is built in: browsers treat output as a live region, meaning screen readers automatically announce its new content when a script updates it. A plain span updated by JavaScript changes silently for a blind user; an output speaks. That single behaviour is the best reason to use the element.

sections.heading: meter: a gauge with judgement zones
sections.body:
The meter element displays a scalar measurement within a known range: disk usage, a test score, password strength, relevance. The essentials are value, min and max — value="0.72" min="0" max="1" renders a bar 72% full. If min and max are omitted they default to 0 and 1.

What elevates meter beyond a styled bar are its judgement attributes: low, high and optimum. They divide the range into zones — below low, between low and high, above high — and optimum declares which zone is desirable. The browser then colours the bar by how far the value sits from the good zone: green when the value is in the optimum region, amber or red as it drifts into bad territory. For disk usage, optimum sits low (empty disk is good), so a value above high renders as a warning without a line of CSS.

Content between the tags — like the text 72% — is fallback for environments that cannot render the gauge, and good practice for accessibility. One firm rule: meter is for measurements at a point in time, and it requires known bounds. It is never for task completion — that is the next element's job.
sections.code:
<label for="disk">Disk usage</label>
<meter id="disk" value="0.72" min="0" max="1"
       low="0.25" high="0.75" optimum="0.1">72%</meter>

sections.heading: progress: how much of the task is done
sections.body:
The progress element reports completion of a task: a file upload, an installation, steps of a wizard. With value and max it renders a determinate bar — value="30" max="100" shows 30% done. min does not exist on progress; the scale always starts at zero, because no task starts 'partially negative'.

Omit the value attribute entirely and the bar becomes indeterminate: an animated sweep meaning 'working, cannot say how far along'. This is the semantically correct spinner for unknown-duration work, and scripts typically start indeterminate, then set value once the total becomes known.

A subtle default bites often: without max, the scale runs 0 to 1. So value="30" alone is clamped to a full bar. Always state max explicitly unless your values genuinely are fractions of one. As with meter, text between the tags serves as fallback.
sections.code:
<label for="backup">Backup</label>
<progress id="backup" value="30" max="100">30%</progress>

<!-- Indeterminate: no value attribute -->
<progress></progress>

sections.heading: meter or progress? The decision rule
sections.body:
Both render horizontal bars, and that visual similarity causes constant misuse. Decide by what the number means, not how it looks. If it answers 'how much of a task has completed and will eventually reach the end?', it is progress. If it answers 'where does this measurement sit within its known range right now?', it is meter.

Disk usage is a meter: the disk is not trying to reach 100%, and 100% is bad. An upload is progress: it marches to completion, and 100% is success. Password strength is a meter; a course-completion tracker is progress. Screen readers announce the two elements differently — 'progress bar, 30%' versus a gauge with its value — so the wrong choice actively misinforms users who cannot see the styling.

When neither fits — say, a decorative skill bar with no real scale — use neither; a styled div lies less than a misused semantic element.

lessons.title: Embed self-hosted video that plays everywhere
lessons.summary: Master the video element: multiple sources with MIME types, controls, autoplay's muted requirement, poster frames, preload strategy and fallback content.
lessons.goal: Embed a product video with two encoded sources, a poster frame, native controls, sensible dimensions and honest fallback text.
lessons.whyItMatters: Video is the heaviest asset most pages ship, and the video element's attributes decide whether it plays smoothly, silently wastes gigabytes of bandwidth, or shows a blank rectangle on half your users' browsers. Understanding source selection, codec compatibility and the autoplay rules keeps your media working across devices — and keeps you out of the browser's autoplay-blocking penalty box.
steps: Read how the browser picks between src and source children, then study the format section.
Add the video element with controls (task 1) and fixed width/height (task 2).
Provide two sources — WebM first, MP4 second — each with its MIME type (tasks 3 and 4).
Set a poster image so the player looks intentional before playback (task 5).
Add fallback text with a download link for unsupported browsers (task 6).
Run the checks, then experiment with muted, autoplay and loop in the preview.
lessons.explanation: The browser walks the source children top to bottom and plays the first format it supports, using the type attribute to decide without downloading anything. WebM comes first as the more efficient codec, MP4 second as the universal safety net. The poster fills the frame before playback, width and height reserve layout space so the page does not jump, and the text inside the element only ever appears in browsers too old to know what video is.
lessons.example:
A page with <video src="demo.avi"> shows a dead grey box for nearly everyone — AVI is not a web format, and single-src markup offers no alternative.

Re-encoded to WebM and MP4 and listed as two typed sources with a poster and controls, the same clip plays natively in every current browser, shows a designed preview frame instead of a black rectangle, and costs users no bandwidth until they press play thanks to preload="metadata".

lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a video player with native controls and a poster frame at 640x360. All six checks pass; the fallback text stays invisible because your browser supports video.
commonMistakes: Using both src on the video tag and source children. The src attribute wins and the alternatives are ignored — pick one mechanism, and use source children when you offer formats.
Writing autoplay without muted. Modern browsers block audible autoplay, so the video simply never starts; autoplay muted (with controls for the sound button) is the working pattern.

Treating the fallback text as an error message for failed loads. It only renders in browsers that do not implement the video element at all — a 404 on the file shows a broken player, not your fallback.
Omitting width and height, causing the page to reflow with a visible jump when video metadata arrives.
lessons.proTip: Order sources by preference, not popularity: put the smaller, more efficient WebM first and MP4 last. Browsers stop at the first playable source, so everyone capable of WebM saves bandwidth and everyone else falls through to MP4.

coding.intro: You will embed a self-hosted product demo the professional way: two codec sources, poster, controls, stable dimensions and a fallback.

sections.heading: The video element and its two source styles
sections.body:
The video element embeds a media player directly in the page. In its simplest form it takes a src attribute pointing at one file: <video src="demo.mp4" controls></video>. That works — as long as every visitor's browser can decode that one file.

The robust form drops the src attribute and nests source elements instead. Each source carries its own src plus a type attribute stating the MIME type, like video/mp4 or video/webm. The browser reads the list top to bottom and commits to the first type it can play. The type attribute is what makes this efficient: without it, the browser must download a chunk of each candidate file to sniff the format; with it, rejection is instant and free.

Never mix the two styles. If the video tag has a src attribute, all source children are ignored. And because selection stops at the first playable source, order expresses preference — put your best-compressed format first.
sections.code:
<!-- One-format shorthand -->
<video src="demo.mp4" controls></video>

<!-- Multi-format, browser picks the first playable -->
<video controls>
  <source src="demo.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="demo.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

sections.heading: Formats and codecs: mp4 and webm
sections.body:
A video file is a container holding separately-encoded video and audio streams, and compatibility depends on both layers. The two containers that matter on the web: MP4 (typically H.264 video with AAC audio), supported effectively everywhere and the universal baseline; and WebM (VP9 or the newer AV1 video with Opus audio), an open, royalty-free format that usually compresses noticeably better, supported by all current browsers but absent from some older Safari versions.

The professional pattern is therefore: encode twice, serve both, WebM first. Users on modern browsers get the smaller file; anyone else falls through to MP4. Formats like AVI, MKV or MOV are not web formats — browsers will not reliably play them regardless of markup, so conversion is a prerequisite, not an option.

One more layer of precision exists when you need it: the type attribute can include a codecs parameter, such as type="video/mp4; codecs=avc1.42E01E". It matters for advanced cases (like offering AV1-in-MP4 with an H.264 fallback) but plain container types cover everyday work.

sections.heading: controls, width and height
sections.body:
The boolean controls attribute asks the browser for its native player chrome: play/pause, a seek bar, volume, fullscreen and (where tracks exist) caption toggles. Without it the video renders with no interface at all — playable only through JavaScript. Unless you are building a fully custom player, controls is effectively mandatory: shipping video a keyboard or screen-reader user cannot operate is an accessibility failure.

width and height set the display size in pixels (write the numbers without units). Their real job is layout stability: stated up front, the browser reserves the correct box immediately, and the page does not lurch when the video's metadata finally reveals its dimensions. Give them the video's intrinsic aspect ratio — a 1280x720 clip belongs in a 16:9 box like 640x360 — or the picture letterboxes inside the element.

CSS can then scale the element responsively (max-width: 100% is typical); the attributes still help by fixing the aspect ratio before any stylesheet loads.
sections.code:
<video controls width="640" height="360">
  <source src="demo.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="demo.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

sections.heading: autoplay, muted and loop
sections.body:
autoplay asks the video to start the moment it can. Browsers, after years of tab-blaring abuse, now enforce a strict policy: audible autoplay is blocked. An autoplaying video must also carry the muted attribute, or most browsers will simply refuse to start it. The working combination for a hero background is autoplay muted loop playsinline — playsinline preventing iOS from hijacking the clip into fullscreen.

muted starts playback with audio off; users can unmute through the controls. loop restarts the video automatically at the end, endlessly — right for short ambient clips, wrong for content people actually watch.

Even correctly-muted autoplay deserves restraint: it burns mobile bandwidth and motion distracts. Reserve it for short, silent, decorative video, and let users start anything with sound themselves.
sections.code:
<!-- Decorative background clip -->
<video autoplay muted loop playsinline width="640" height="360">
  <source src="ambient.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="ambient.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

sections.heading: poster and preload
sections.body:
Before playback begins, an unstyled video shows either a black box or its first frame — often a mid-blink face. The poster attribute replaces that with a chosen image: a title card, a clean keyframe, a designed thumbnail. It costs one image request and transforms how deliberate the page looks.

preload tells the browser how much to fetch before the user presses play. Its three values: none (fetch nothing — cheapest, best for pages where playback is unlikely), metadata (fetch just duration and dimensions, a few kilobytes — the sensible default for most pages), and auto (the browser may buffer aggressively, appropriate only when playback is near-certain). An autoplay attribute makes preload moot, since the whole video is needed immediately.

Together they define your bandwidth ethics: poster plus preload="metadata" gives users a rich-looking player that costs almost nothing until they opt in.
sections.code:
<video controls width="640" height="360"
       poster="preview.jpg" preload="metadata">
  <source src="demo.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="demo.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

sections.heading: Fallback content: for whom, exactly
sections.body:
Anything inside the video element after the source children is fallback content, rendered only by browsers that do not implement the video element at all. Every current browser does implement it, so this text serves ancient browsers, some text-mode agents, and — importantly — anywhere your HTML gets reproduced outside a browser, like an email client or a feed reader.

Understand what fallback is not: it is not an error handler. If the files 404 or every source format is unsupported, a video-capable browser shows a broken player, not your fallback text. Handling that gracefully requires JavaScript listening for error events.

Make the fallback useful rather than scolding. 'Your browser does not support HTML video' helps nobody by itself; add a direct download link to the MP4 so the person can still watch the content some other way. A one-line fallback with a link is the professional standard.

lessons.title: Publish audio with captions using audio, source and track
lessons.summary: Embed sound with the audio element and its source fallbacks, then make media accessible with WebVTT text tracks for captions, subtitles and descriptions.
lessons.goal: Embed a podcast episode with two audio formats, a sensible preload strategy, and a captions track wired up with kind, srclang, label and default.
lessons.whyItMatters: Audio embedding looks trivial until you meet the details: which formats actually decode everywhere, why autoplaying sound gets your page muted by the browser, and how much bandwidth preload silently spends. The track element is the other half of professional media work — captions are a legal accessibility requirement in many contexts, and WebVTT is the format every browser understands. Together these skills let you ship media that everyone can use.
steps: Read the audio element theory, then the format comparison.
Add the audio player with controls (task 1).
Provide MP3 and OGG sources with MIME types (tasks 2 and 3).
Set preload="metadata" so the page stays light (task 4).
Study the WebVTT section, then attach a captions track with kind, srclang, label and default (task 5).
Add fallback text with a download link (task 6) and run the checks.
lessons.explanation: The browser tries the OGG source first and falls back to MP3, choosing by the type attribute without downloading either. preload="metadata" fetches only the duration until the user presses play. The track element points at a WebVTT file: kind="captions" says it transcribes speech plus meaningful sounds, srclang declares the text language, label names it in the player menu, and default switches it on automatically.
lessons.example:
A podcast page with a bare link to episode.mp3 forces users into their download folder, and deaf visitors get nothing at all.

The same episode inside an audio element plays right on the page with native controls, streams only metadata until requested, and carries an English captions track — so a user in a loud train, or one who cannot hear, reads the conversation as it plays.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, build the podcast player: a controlled audio element with OGG and MP3 typed sources, metadata-only preloading, a fully-attributed captions track and a fallback download link.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a compact native audio player. All six checks pass; the captions track and fallback are present in the markup even though the audio bar itself looks minimal.
commonMistakes: Writing type="audio/mp3". The registered MIME type for MP3 is audio/mpeg — audio/mp3 is a common guess that some browsers tolerate and others do not.
Autoplaying audio. Browsers block audible autoplay outright, and unlike video there is no useful muted-autoplay pattern for sound — let users press play.
Marking a track default without checking kind. A default subtitles track switches on translation for everyone; captions as default is usually the safer choice.
Forgetting that WebVTT files must start with the exact header line WEBVTT — without it the whole track silently fails to parse.
lessons.proTip: Captions versus subtitles is an intent distinction, not a technical one: captions serve people who cannot hear the audio (they include sounds like [door slams]), subtitles serve people who cannot understand the language. Choose kind accordingly — screen readers and player menus present them differently.

sections.heading: The audio element
sections.body:
The audio element embeds a sound player. With the controls attribute it renders the browser's compact native bar — play/pause, a timeline, volume — and without controls it is invisible and inert until JavaScript drives it. Like video, it accepts either a single src attribute or nested source children, and the same rule applies: an src attribute on the audio tag makes the browser ignore every source child.

The attribute set mirrors video where it makes sense: autoplay, loop, muted, preload all exist. loop is genuinely useful for ambience in web apps; muted on audio is mostly a scripting tool, since a muted sound player serves little purpose to humans.

Content inside the element after the sources is fallback, shown only by agents that do not implement audio at all — same contract as video, same best practice: one honest sentence plus a download link.

sections.heading: Audio formats: mp3, ogg, wav
sections.body:
Three formats cover web audio. MP3 (MIME type audio/mpeg — note, not audio/mp3) is the universal baseline: lossy, small, decodable by every browser in use. If you ship only one format, ship MP3.

OGG (audio/ogg, usually containing the Vorbis or Opus codec) is the open alternative: royalty-free and typically better quality per kilobyte than MP3, especially with Opus. Historical Safari versions lacked it, which is why OGG is offered first with MP3 beneath, never alone.

WAV (audio/wav) is essentially uncompressed PCM: perfect fidelity at brutal size — a minute of CD-quality WAV weighs around ten megabytes. It has niche uses (tiny UI sounds, audio-editing tools) but is the wrong choice for music or speech delivery. As with video, list sources in preference order and always include the type attribute so browsers can reject formats without downloading them.
sections.code:
<audio controls>
  <source src="clip.ogg" type="audio/ogg">
  <source src="clip.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
  <source src="clip.wav" type="audio/wav">
</audio>

sections.heading: autoplay pitfalls and preload strategy
sections.body:
Autoplaying sound is the most-hated behaviour on the web, and browsers have codified the hatred: audible autoplay is blocked by default in every major browser. An audio element with autoplay will usually just not start, and pages that fight the policy with scripts get their whole tab muted by the browser UI. Unlike video, audio has no meaningful silent-autoplay use, so the practical rule is simple: never autoplay audio; let the user press play.

preload manages the cost of the player before anyone interacts. none fetches nothing — right for pages listing fifty episodes where loading fifty files would be absurd. metadata fetches just enough to show duration — the best default for a typical single-episode page. auto invites the browser to buffer the whole file — defensible only when playback is nearly certain.

A subtlety worth knowing: preload is a hint, not a command. Browsers may fetch less than requested on metered connections or when many players share a page. Design as if preload were advisory — because it is.
sections.code:
<!-- Episode list: pay nothing until a user chooses -->
<audio controls preload="none">
  <source src="ep42.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
</audio>

sections.heading: The track element: text for your media
sections.body:
The track element attaches a timed text file to an audio or video element. It is a void element placed inside the media element after the sources, and its kind attribute declares the text's purpose: subtitles (translation or transcription for people who do not understand the language), captions (transcription plus meaningful non-speech sounds, for people who cannot hear the audio), descriptions (a spoken-by-screen-reader account of important visuals, for blind users), chapters (named navigation points), and metadata (machine-readable cues for scripts, never displayed).

Three more attributes complete the wiring. srclang states the language of the track text as a language code like en or el — required when kind is subtitles, wise always. label gives the human name shown in the player's caption menu, like 'English' or 'Greek'. The boolean default marks the one track per kind that should be enabled without user action.

A player can hold several tracks — English captions, Greek subtitles, chapter markers — and the native controls grow a menu to switch between them. For audio elements specifically, browser UI support for showing captions is weaker than for video; many podcast sites also render the transcript as visible page text, which helps SEO too.
sections.code:
<video controls width="640" height="360">
  <source src="talk.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="talk.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track src="talk-en.vtt" kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  <track src="talk-el.vtt" kind="subtitles" srclang="el" label="Greek">
</video>

sections.heading: WebVTT in five minutes
sections.body:
The file a track points at is WebVTT — Web Video Text Tracks — a plain-text format with a .vtt extension. Its grammar is small: the file must begin with the literal line WEBVTT, followed by a blank line, then any number of cues. Each cue is an optional identifier line, a timing line of the form 00:00:01.000 --> 00:00:04.500 (start and end, with a period before milliseconds), and one or more lines of text, all separated from the next cue by a blank line.

Cue text may contain simple markup — <b>, <i>, and voice spans like <v Maria> to name speakers — and captions conventionally put sound effects in square brackets: [phone buzzes]. Timing must be sequential within a cue (end after start), and overlapping cues are allowed for dialogue.

Two operational details cause most real-world failures: the header line must be exactly WEBVTT (a missing header kills the entire track with no visible error), and when the page and the .vtt file live on different origins, the media element needs crossorigin handling — same-origin hosting is the simple path.
sections.code:
WEBVTT

1
00:00:01.000 --> 00:00:04.500
<v Host>Welcome back to the show.

2
00:00:04.800 --> 00:00:07.000
[intro music fades]

sections.heading: Choosing kinds, and why captions are not optional
sections.body:
Pick kind by who is served. A viewer who cannot hear needs captions — the speech plus the [door slams] that a subtitles file would omit. A viewer who hears fine but speaks another language needs subtitles. A blind viewer of video needs descriptions of what happens on screen. Publishing a lecture series? chapters tracks turn a one-hour file into navigable sections.

Captions carry legal weight: accessibility legislation in many jurisdictions (and procurement rules in many organisations) require captioned media. Beyond compliance, captions are used far past their target audience — people in open offices, language learners, anyone in a loud or silent environment. Studies of social platforms consistently show most video is watched muted.

The markup cost, as you have seen, is one line per track plus a text file. There is no cheaper accessibility win anywhere in HTML.

lessons.title: Embed other pages safely with iframes
lessons.summary: Master the iframe element: required titles, lazy loading, the sandbox permission system, named frames as link targets, and the security realities of third-party embeds.
lessons.goal: Build a dashboard that embeds an external page with a title, lazy loading, dimensions and a sandbox, plus a named frame driven by links.
lessons.whyItMatters: Iframes power the embedded maps, videos and payment widgets on virtually every commercial site — a page inside your page, with its own document and its own security context. Used carelessly they are also a classic attack surface: an unsandboxed third-party frame runs someone else's code adjacent to your users. Knowing title, loading, sandbox and the framing headers is the difference between embedding responsibly and embedding dangerously.
steps: Read what an iframe actually is — a nested browsing context, not a fancy image.
Embed the status page with src and an accessible title (task 1), then size it (task 2).
Defer offscreen loading with loading="lazy" (task 3).
Restrict the embed's powers with a sandbox allowing only scripts (task 4).
Create the named preview frame (task 5) and point a link at it with target (task 6).
Read the security section, then run all checks.

lessons.explanation: The first iframe embeds an external status page: title describes it for screen-reader users (who otherwise hear just 'frame'), width and height reserve stable space, loading="lazy" defers the fetch until the frame nears the viewport, and sandbox strips every capability except the two explicitly allowed. The second pattern uses name: links elsewhere on the page target the frame by that name, so clicking Report B loads it inside the frame instead of navigating the whole tab.
lessons.example:
A dashboard that links out to the status page loses the user to another tab; pasting the status HTML into your page is impossible since you do not control it.

An iframe threads the needle: the live external page renders inside a 600x400 region of your dashboard, isolated in its own browsing context, loading lazily below the fold, and — because it is third-party content — locked in a sandbox that removes popups, form submission and top-level navigation.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, complete the dashboard: an embedded status page with title, dimensions, lazy loading and a sandbox, then a named preview frame with two links that load reports into it.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows the sandboxed status frame and a report frame that swaps content when the two links are clicked. All six checks pass.
commonMistakes: Shipping iframes without title. Screen readers announce an untitled frame as just 'frame', leaving users to guess; title is effectively mandatory for accessibility.

Writing sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" on a frame whose content you also serve — that combination lets framed code reach up and remove its own sandbox. For same-origin content, question whether you need sandbox at all.
Expecting any site to be embeddable. Sites send X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors headers to refuse framing — google.com in an iframe renders a blank refusal, and that is by design.
Lazy-loading an iframe at the top of the page. loading="lazy" on above-the-fold content delays what users see first; reserve it for frames below the fold.
lessons.proTip: Never build a login or checkout form inside a third-party iframe context you do not fully control, and prefer embedding via the provider's documented embed URL (like youtube.com/embed/ID) — those endpoints are designed and hardened for framing, unlike normal site pages.

sections.heading: What an iframe really is
sections.body:
An iframe (inline frame) embeds one complete HTML document inside another. The framed page is not merged into yours: it is a separate browsing context with its own document, its own styles, its own scripts and its own security origin. Your CSS cannot reach into it, and — when the origins differ — its scripts cannot reach out to your page either. That isolation is exactly why iframes are the standard vehicle for third-party widgets.

The src attribute names the document to load. Two sizing attributes, width and height, set the viewport in pixels; like images and videos, stating them prevents layout shift. The frame shows scrollbars automatically when the inner document overflows.

One attribute is non-negotiable: title. A screen reader reaching an untitled iframe can only announce 'frame' — the user has no idea whether it holds a map, an ad or their bank balance. A short description like title="Live service status" fixes it. Treat a missing iframe title as an error, because accessibility audits will.
sections.code:
<iframe src="https://status.example.com"
        title="Live service status"
        width="600" height="400"></iframe>

sections.heading: loading="lazy" and frame performance
sections.body:
Iframes are expensive: each one loads a whole page — HTML, CSS, scripts, images — and historically all of it loaded up front, even for frames three screens below the fold. The loading attribute fixes this: loading="lazy" tells the browser to defer fetching the frame until the user scrolls near it, while loading="eager" (the default) loads immediately.

The rule of thumb mirrors images: lazy-load everything below the fold, eager-load anything visible at page open. A lazily-loaded map at the bottom of a contact page can cut hundreds of kilobytes and multiple third-party connections from the initial load.

Because a deferred frame occupies zero network time until needed, always pair loading="lazy" with explicit width and height — otherwise the page reflows twice: once at first paint, again when the frame finally materialises.
sections.code:
<!-- Bottom of a long page -->
<iframe src="https://maps.example.com/embed?q=office"
        title="Map of our office"
        width="600" height="450" loading="lazy"></iframe>

sections.heading: sandbox: a permission system for embeds
sections.body:
The sandbox attribute strips the framed document of nearly every capability, then lets you add specific ones back as space-separated tokens. A bare sandbox="" is maximum restriction: no scripts, no form submission, no popups, no navigation of your page, no plugins, and the content is forced into a unique opaque origin (so it cannot use cookies or storage even from its own site).

The important tokens: allow-scripts re-enables JavaScript; allow-forms permits form submission; allow-popups lets it open windows; allow-same-origin lets the content keep its real origin instead of the opaque one, restoring its cookies and storage; allow-top-navigation lets the frame navigate your whole tab (rarely wise); allow-modals re-enables alert/confirm dialogs; allow-downloads permits downloads. You grant the minimum set the embed needs to function — a widget that only draws needs allow-scripts and nothing else.

One dangerous combination to memorise: allow-scripts plus allow-same-origin on content from your own origin means the framed script can reach into the parent and remove its own sandbox attribute — the sandbox becomes decoration. For genuinely third-party content the pair is common and acceptable (the cross-origin wall still stands); for same-origin content it defeats the purpose.
sections.code:
<!-- Third-party widget: scripts only, nothing else -->
<iframe src="https://widget.example.com/chart"
        title="Market chart" width="400" height="300"
        sandbox="allow-scripts"></iframe>

sections.heading: allow and allowfullscreen: granting device features
sections.body:
Separate from sandbox, the allow attribute controls which powerful browser features the framed page may use — camera, microphone, geolocation, autoplay, clipboard and more. Each feature is named with an allowlist, semicolon-separated: allow="camera; microphone" for a video-call widget, allow="autoplay; fullscreen" for a media player. Features not granted are denied inside the frame regardless of what the inner page requests.

allowfullscreen is the older boolean that permits the framed content to enter fullscreen — you still see it everywhere because YouTube's embed code includes it. Modern syntax expresses the same thing as allow="fullscreen", and including both harms nothing.

The division of labour: sandbox takes capabilities away from untrusted content, allow grants sensitive device features to trusted content. A well-defended embed often carries both, each list as short as possible.
sections.code:
<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/VIDEO_ID"
        title="Product launch keynote"
        width="560" height="315"
        allow="autoplay; fullscreen; picture-in-picture"
        allowfullscreen></iframe>

sections.heading: Named frames as link targets
sections.body:
Give an iframe a name attribute and it becomes a navigation target: any link whose target matches that name loads its href inside the frame instead of the current tab. No JavaScript involved — this is the same target mechanism as target="_blank", pointed at a frame instead of a new tab.

The pattern builds instant master-detail interfaces: a list of report links on the left, a single named frame on the right, each click swapping the frame's document. Forms can do the same with target on the form element, submitting into a frame.

Give the frame an initial src so the region is never blank, and remember the frame still needs its title — name is for the linking machinery, title for humans. If no frame matches a link's target name, the browser opens a new tab with that name, which is almost never what you wanted; keep names and targets in exact sync.

sections.heading: Embedding YouTube and maps properly
sections.body:
Big platforms publish dedicated embed endpoints, and using them matters. YouTube videos embed via https://www.youtube.com/embed/VIDEO_ID — not the watch URL, which refuses framing. The embed endpoint serves a page designed for iframes: minimal chrome, the player API, correct framing headers. Map providers work the same way, offering an 'embed' or 'share' snippet that wraps a purpose-built URL in an iframe with sensible attributes.

When you paste a provider's snippet, still audit it against this lesson: does it carry a title (usually you must add one)? Should it be loading="lazy" (usually yes, below the fold)? Are the width and height right for your layout?

A note on the legacy elements you will meet in old code: object (with a data attribute) and embed were the pre-iframe ways to include external resources like PDFs and Flash content. object still has a niche for inline PDFs, but for embedding web content both are obsolete — new work uses iframe, full stop.
sections.code:
<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/dQw4w9WgXcQ"
        title="Launch video" width="560" height="315"
        loading="lazy" allowfullscreen></iframe>

<!-- Legacy, for recognition only -->
<object data="manual.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="600" height="800"></object>

sections.heading: Why third-party frames demand care
sections.body:
Framing runs in both directions, and both have security stakes. When you embed others: the framed page executes its own scripts with its own origin's cookies. Inside an unsandboxed frame it can open popups, start downloads, navigate your tab to a phishing page, or mine cryptocurrency. Every third-party iframe is a trust decision — sandbox it to the minimum, and only embed origins you would vouch for.

When others embed you: a hostile site can frame your page invisibly and trick users into clicking your buttons — the attack called clickjacking. Defence happens in HTTP headers your server sends: the legacy X-Frame-Options header (DENY or SAMEORIGIN), and its modern successor, the CSP frame-ancestors directive, which can name exactly which origins may frame you. This is why most login pages refuse to render inside your iframe — their servers forbid framing, correctly.

The takeaway for an HTML author: expect embeds of serious sites to fail unless they offer an embed endpoint, protect your own sensitive pages with framing headers (a server configuration task to raise with your team), and treat sandbox as seatbelt-mandatory for any frame whose content you do not control.
