lessons.title: Document code the right way with code, pre, kbd, samp and var
lessons.summary: Use HTML's five computer-text elements with their exact semantics, escape angle brackets with entities, and present multi-line listings that survive whitespace.
lessons.goal: Mark up a small API documentation page with inline code, an escaped multi-line listing, keyboard shortcuts, sample output and variable placeholders.
lessons.whyItMatters: Technical documentation lives or dies on precise code presentation. Browsers collapse whitespace by default, so unprepared code listings flatten into soup; raw angle brackets get parsed as tags and vanish. The five computer-text elements — each with a distinct meaning — plus entity escaping are the toolkit behind every readable docs page, README render and developer blog on the web.
steps: Read the semantics of each of the five elements first — they are not interchangeable.
Wrap the inline function name in <code> (task 1).
Build the multi-line listing with the pre>code pattern (task 2).
Escape the angle brackets in the HTML sample with entities (task 3).
Mark the keyboard shortcut with kbd elements (task 4).
Mark the program output with samp (task 5) and the placeholder with var (task 6), then run the checks.
lessons.prompt:
Call fetchUser(id), press Ctrl + Enter, and the console prints User loaded.

<section>
  <h2>Results</h2>
</section>
lessons.explanation: Each element states what kind of computer text it wraps: code for source fragments, var for a placeholder the reader replaces, kbd for keys the user presses, samp for what the machine prints back. The listing combines pre (preserve whitespace and line breaks) with code (this is source), and its angle brackets are written as < and > entities so the browser displays them instead of parsing them as real tags.
lessons.example:
A docs page written with plain paragraphs renders 'call fetchUser(id) and press Ctrl Enter' as indistinguishable prose, and its example markup disappears entirely because the browser parsed the tags.

The same page with the five elements shows the function in monospace, the keys as keycap-styled tokens, the output visually distinct from the input, and the HTML example displayed exactly as written, indentation intact.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, convert a flat documentation snippet into proper computer-text markup: inline code, a pre>code listing with escaped brackets, kbd keys, samp output and a var placeholder.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows monospace inline fragments, an indented multi-line code block displaying literal angle brackets, and distinct keyboard/output styling. All six checks pass.
commonMistakes: Using pre alone for code. pre only means 'preserve whitespace' — the pre>code combination states both formatting and meaning, and is what syntax highlighters target.
Leaving raw < and > inside code samples. The browser parses them as real tags: your example markup vanishes from the page and may even break its layout. Escape as < and >.
Wrapping a whole shortcut in one kbd. Each key gets its own element — <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd> — so styling and screen readers treat the keys individually.
Using code for output or samp for input. code is what a human writes for the machine; samp is what the machine prints back — mixing them misleads readers scanning for what to type.
lessons.proTip: Indentation inside pre starts at the source: any leading spaces you use to indent the pre block itself in your HTML file become visible output. Docs authors conventionally left-align the content of pre against column zero, even when it breaks the file's indentation rhythm.

coding.intro: You will mark up a mini documentation page for a JavaScript function, exercising all five computer-text elements and entity escaping.

sections.heading: code: fragments of source
sections.body:
The code element marks a fragment of computer code: a function name, a filename, an HTML tag name, a JSON key, a shell command. Browsers render it in the system monospace font, but as always the styling is a side effect — the meaning is 'this token belongs to a machine language, not to English'.

Use it inline and liberally in technical prose: every identifier mentioned mid-sentence belongs in code. Beyond consistent styling, this gives CSS a single hook (code { ... }) to restyle every fragment site-wide, and helps tools — from search indexers to screen readers with verbosity settings — treat the tokens correctly.

code carries no line-break behaviour of its own. Inline it flows with the sentence; for multi-line listings it partners with pre, covered next.
sections.code: The filter() method returns a new array; configure it in settings.json.

sections.heading: pre, and the pre>code pattern
sections.body:
HTML collapses whitespace: any run of spaces, tabs and newlines in your source renders as a single space. Essential for prose, fatal for code — a carefully indented listing flattens onto one line. The pre element (preformatted text) switches that off: inside pre, every space and line break renders exactly as written, in monospace. pre alone says only 'preserve my formatting'; it is equally valid for ASCII diagrams or poetry. To say 'this preserved block is source code', nest code inside: 
...
. This pairing is the standard idiom across documentation tooling, and syntax-highlighting libraries target it by convention, often via a class like language-js on the code element. One mechanical detail: the preservation applies to your HTML source itself. A line break immediately after the opening 
 becomes a visible blank first line, and the indentation your editor adds to nested markup becomes visible leading space. Start the content flush against the opening tags.
sections.code:
function greet(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}`;
}

sections.heading: Escaping < and > inside code samples
sections.body:
Here is the trap every documentation author hits once: put example HTML inside a code block, and it disappears. The browser has no way to know your <section> was meant as display text — it parses it as a real element, renders it, and your 'code sample' becomes invisible structure.

The fix is character entities: write < for < and > for >. The browser renders the symbols but never parses them as markup. Strictly, only < requires escaping (a bare > is usually harmless), but escaping both is the professional habit — symmetry makes samples easier to audit. And if your sample itself contains entities you want shown literally, escape the ampersand too: &lt; renders as the four characters <.

This is tedious by hand, which is why real documentation pipelines (Markdown renderers, static site generators) escape automatically. But generators fail, snippets get pasted, and when a code sample mysteriously vanishes from a page, unescaped brackets are the first thing to check.
sections.code:
<article>
  <h2>Title</h2>
  <p>Body text.</p>
</article>

sections.heading: kbd: what the user presses
sections.body: The kbd element marks user input — most commonly keyboard keys, by extension anything the user enters or activates: menu paths, spoken commands, button names in instructions. Browsers render it monospace; documentation sites usually add CSS to draw each kbd as a keycap with a border and shadow. The composition convention: one kbd per key, punctuation between them outside the elements — Ctrl + Shift + P. This keeps each keycap individually styleable and reads correctly in assistive tech. The specification also blesses nesting for whole shortcuts (a kbd wrapping kbds), but per-key elements joined by plus signs is the pattern you will see and write. Distinguish intent: git status is a command as a piece of text; 'type git status and press Enter' is the user performing input. The overlap is real, and the deciding question is whether you are naming a token or instructing an action.
sections.code: Open the palette with Ctrl + Shift + P, then press Enter.

sections.heading: samp: what the machine says back
sections.body:
The samp element marks sample output from a program: a console line, an error message, a status response. It is the mirror image of kbd — kbd flows from human to machine, samp from machine to human — and both default to monospace, so without semantic markup readers cannot tell command from result.

That distinction is the whole value. In a terminal transcript, the reader must know which lines to type and which to expect. Docs sites often style samp differently (dimmed, or prefixed visually) precisely to carry that difference; the semantics make it possible.

The elements nest to express interleaving: a pre block can contain kbd lines (what you typed) alternating with samp lines (what came back). And samp may contain kbd for echoed input, or code when output happens to be code. Choose by direction of flow and the transcript stays honest.

sections.heading: var, and choosing between the five
sections.body:
The var element marks a variable or placeholder: a mathematical variable (<var>x</var>), a named quantity in prose, or — its docs superpower — the part of an example the reader must replace with their own value. In a usage line like ssh <var>user</var>@<var>host</var>, the var elements say 'these two words are yours to substitute; the rest is literal'. Browsers render var in italics by default.

A quick decision guide for documentation pages: naming a token of code, a file, a tag, a command? code. Showing a multi-line listing? pre>code, with entities for any angle brackets. Telling the user which keys to press or what to type? kbd. Quoting what the program printed? samp. Marking the substitutable part of any of the above? var, nested where needed.

Five elements, five directions of meaning. Pages that use them correctly can restyle all code presentation from one stylesheet, feed accurate structure to assistive technology, and never leave a reader guessing whether a monospace word is input, output or placeholder.

lessons.title: Make any page mobile-ready with the responsive fundamentals
lessons.summary: Set up the viewport meta tag, make images fluid, size text in relative units, and understand where media queries and srcset fit in the responsive toolkit.
lessons.goal: Convert a fixed desktop-era page into one that renders correctly on a phone: correct viewport, fluid images, rem-based text and a first media query.
lessons.whyItMatters: More than half of all web traffic is mobile, and a page without responsive foundations renders on a phone as a zoomed-out desktop miniature with microscopic text. One meta tag, one image rule and a habit of relative units fix ninety percent of that — before any advanced CSS. These fundamentals are also assumed knowledge for every CSS framework and every job interview that mentions 'mobile-first'.
steps: Read what the viewport meta tag does and what breaks without it.
Add the viewport tag with width=device-width and initial-scale=1 (tasks 1 and 2).
Make the hero image fluid with the max-width pattern (tasks 3 and 4).
Convert the fixed pixel font size to rem (task 5).
Read the media-query and srcset sections, add the min-width query (task 6), and run the checks.
Open your browser DevTools device mode and watch the page adapt.
lessons.prompt:
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

<style>
  body { font-size: 1rem; }
  img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
  @media (min-width: 40rem) {
    body { font-size: 1.125rem; }
  }
</style>
lessons.explanation: The viewport tag tells mobile browsers to lay the page out at the device's real width instead of a simulated 980px desktop canvas, and initial-scale=1 opens it at 100% zoom. The image rule lets pictures shrink with their container but never overflow it, height auto preserving their proportions. Text in rem scales with the user's browser setting, and the media query adds a size bump only when the viewport is wide enough.
lessons.example:
Open a viewport-less page on a phone: the browser pretends the screen is 980px wide, renders a tiny desktop layout, and the user pinch-zooms to read every paragraph. A 1600px hero image forces horizontal scrolling on top of that.

After the fixes, the same page opens at readable size, the hero shrinks to fit the screen edge-to-edge, text respects the user's font preferences, and wider screens get comfortably larger type — all from a handful of lines.

lessons.expectedResult: In the preview (and especially in DevTools device mode) the page fills small screens without horizontal scrolling, the image scales with the window, and all six checks pass.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the viewport tag entirely — the single most common reason a 'finished' site looks broken on phones. No CSS can compensate for the wrong viewport.

Blocking zoom with user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1. Users with low vision depend on pinch zoom; disabling it is an accessibility violation, and modern browsers increasingly ignore the restriction anyway.
Writing width:100% instead of max-width:100% on images. Full width stretches small images past their natural size into blur; max-width only ever shrinks.
Sizing text in px everywhere. Pixel-locked text ignores the user's chosen browser font size; rem respects it and scales the whole page proportionally.
lessons.proTip: In Chrome or Firefox DevTools, toggle device mode (the phone icon, Ctrl+Shift+M) and test at 320px width — the narrowest common phone. If nothing overflows horizontally at 320px, your page survives almost any real device.

coding.intro: You will take a page built for 2005-era desktops and give it the four responsive fundamentals: viewport, fluid images, relative units and a first media query.

sections.heading: The viewport meta tag — and what breaks without it
sections.body:
When smartphones arrived, the web was full of desktop-only pages, so mobile browsers adopted a survival trick: pretend the screen is a desktop-sized canvas (roughly 980px wide), render the page onto it, then shrink the whole picture to fit the physical screen. Every page 'worked' — as an unreadable miniature the user zooms around.

That legacy behaviour is still the default. The viewport meta tag is how you opt out: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> in the head. width=device-width says 'lay out at the device's real CSS width' (around 360-430px on typical phones), and initial-scale=1 says 'open at 100% zoom'. With it, your text renders at readable size and your responsive CSS actually has a small viewport to respond to.

Without it, nothing else in this lesson functions: media queries never see a narrow width because the browser is simulating a wide one. Every page you ship should carry this exact tag — it is boilerplate in the best sense.
sections.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>My page</title>
</head>

sections.heading: Viewport values you should and should not use
sections.body:
The content attribute takes comma-separated directives. Beyond the essential two, you will encounter: minimum-scale and maximum-scale (bounds on zoom), and user-scalable=no (disable pinch zoom entirely).

Treat the zoom-restricting ones as forbidden in normal work. Low-vision users rely on pinch zoom to read; locking it out is an accessibility failure serious enough that iOS Safari deliberately ignores user-scalable=no. The rare legitimate exceptions (a full-screen drawing app where pinch means something else) are exactly that — rare.

You may also see width set to a fixed number like width=600 in old code, forcing a specific layout width. It solves nothing that device-width plus fluid design does not solve better. The modern rule fits on a sticky note: always width=device-width, initial-scale=1, and nothing that restricts the user's zoom.
sections.code:
<!-- Correct, always -->
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

<!-- Accessibility violation: do not ship -->
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, user-scalable=no">

sections.heading: Fluid images: the max-width pattern
sections.body:
Images have fixed intrinsic sizes, and a 1600px photo in a 360px viewport means horizontal scrolling — the definitive symptom of a non-responsive page. The universal fix is one CSS rule: img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }.

Unpack it: max-width: 100% lets an image render at its natural size when space allows, but never wider than its container — on a narrow phone it shrinks to fit. height: auto keeps the shrunken image's proportions; without it, an HTML height attribute would hold the old fixed height and the picture would squash.

Note what max-width does that width: 100% does not: it only ever shrinks. A 200px icon stays 200px instead of being inflated to fill a 1200px column as a blurry mess. Keep writing width and height attributes in the HTML — the browser uses their ratio to reserve space before the image loads, preventing layout jumps — and let this CSS rule govern the final rendered size.

sections.heading: Relative units: % and rem
sections.body:
Fixed pixel sizes fight responsiveness; relative units cooperate with it. Percentages size boxes relative to their parent — a sidebar at width: 30% occupies thirty percent of whatever its container currently is, on any screen. This is the oldest responsive tool and still the backbone of fluid layout.

rem sizes relative to the root font size — 1rem equals the html element's font size, which is 16px by default but crucially follows the user's browser preference. Text set in rem scales when a user bumps their default font size; text locked in px ignores them. Sizing text, spacing and even media-query breakpoints in rem makes the entire design scale as one system.

You will also meet em (relative to the current element's own font size — useful, but it compounds through nesting in ways that surprise) and viewport units like vw and vh (percent of the viewport itself). A practical starting policy: rem for text and spacing, percentages for fluid boxes, px only for genuinely fixed details like a 1px border.
sections.code:
<style>
  body { font-size: 1rem; }      /* = user's preferred size */
  h1   { font-size: 2rem; }      /* always double body text */
  .col { width: 50%; }           /* half of the parent, any screen */
</style>

sections.heading: Media queries: the concept in one section
sections.body:
Fluid sizing bends a layout; media queries restructure it. A media query is a CSS block applied only when a condition about the environment holds — most commonly viewport width: @media (min-width: 40rem) { ... } applies its rules only on viewports at least that wide.

The mobile-first discipline: write your base CSS for the narrowest screen, then add min-width queries that progressively enhance wider ones — more columns, larger type, revealed sidebars. The widths where design changes are called breakpoints, and good practice derives them from where your content starts looking wrong, not from a list of device names.

Media queries are CSS territory, and this HTML course only opens the door — the CSS path teaches layout switching in depth. What belongs to HTML is the enabling contract you have already built: without the viewport meta tag, a phone reports the fake 980px width and your min-width queries match wrongly. HTML sets the stage; CSS performs.
sections.code:
<style>
  /* Base: narrow screens */
  body { font-size: 1rem; }

  /* Enhancement: wider screens */
  @media (min-width: 40rem) {
    body { font-size: 1.125rem; }
  }
</style>

sections.heading: srcset teaser, and testing in DevTools
sections.body:
The fluid-image rule scales one file for every screen — a phone downloads the same 1600px hero it shows at 360px, wasting most of the bytes. HTML's answer is the srcset attribute (with sizes, and the picture element for art direction): you list the same image at several widths and the browser downloads only the size the situation needs. It deserves its own lesson, and the advanced responsive-images lesson in this course covers it fully — for now, know that fluid display and efficient delivery are separate problems, and today you solved the first.

Testing is where responsiveness becomes real. Every desktop browser's DevTools includes a device mode (in Chrome and Firefox: the phone icon, or Ctrl+Shift+M / Cmd+Shift+M) that renders your page at chosen device dimensions, simulates touch, and can throttle the network. Drag the viewport edge and watch your breakpoints engage.

A sanity checklist to run in device mode before calling any page done: no horizontal scrollbar at 320px, text readable without zooming, images inside their containers, and tap targets not crowded together. Five minutes of device-mode checking catches what a maximised desktop window never will.

lessons.title: Capstone: build a complete event registration form
lessons.summary: Combine everything from the forms lessons — semantic structure, fieldsets, every major control type and validation — into one production-shaped registration page.
lessons.goal: Ship a full conference registration form: semantic skeleton, grouped fieldsets, labelled personal fields, radio and checkbox groups, a grouped select, date and textarea inputs, and working validation.
lessons.whyItMatters: Registration forms are where every forms concept meets reality at once: structure, grouping, labelling, control choice and validation all interact, and a weakness in any one shows up as bad data or abandoned signups. This capstone is deliberately shaped like a ticket you would receive at work — building it end to end proves you can plan a form, not just recite its elements.
steps: Read the planning sections first: fields, then grouping, then labels, then validation, then submission.
Set up the form with method="post" and its submit button (task 1).
Build the personal-details fieldset with labelled name, email and phone inputs (task 2).
Add the ticket-type radio group in its own fieldset (task 3).
Add the workshop checkboxes and the grouped session select (task 4).
Add the arrival date and dietary-notes textarea (task 5), then finish the validation layer (task 6) and run all checks.
lessons.prompt:
<form action="/register" method="post">
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Personal details</legend>
    <label for="name">Full name</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required autocomplete="name">
    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required autocomplete="email">
    <label for="phone">Phone</label>
    <input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone" pattern="[0-9 +-]{7,15}"
           title="7 to 15 digits, spaces, + or - allowed">
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Register</button>
</form>
lessons.explanation: The form posts its data because registrations change server state and contain personal information — never GET. The fieldset/legend pair names the group for everyone, including screen readers that announce 'Personal details' before each field. Every input is tied to a visible label by for/id, required marks the fields the process cannot proceed without, and the phone pattern comes with a title so its error message explains the expected format.
lessons.example:
The ticket: 'Registration page for DevConf — collect attendee details, ticket type, optional workshops, session preference, arrival date and dietary needs.'

Planned as markup: personal details become labelled text/email/tel inputs in one fieldset; the one-of-three ticket choice becomes radios in a second fieldset; multi-choice workshops become checkboxes; the long session list becomes a select with optgroups; arrival is a date input; dietary needs a textarea. Required and pattern attributes encode the business rules, and a single submit button posts the lot.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, complete the DevConf registration form task by task: form setup, personal fieldset, ticket radios, workshops and session select, date and textarea, then the validation pass.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a fully structured registration form with two boxed field groups; submitting it empty triggers validation on name and email, and a malformed phone number shows the pattern hint. All six checks pass.
commonMistakes: Using method="get" for a registration. Personal data would appear in the URL, get logged and cached, and GET signals a read, not a state change — registrations are POST.
Giving the radio buttons different name values. Radios only become mutually exclusive when they share one name; different names let users select several ticket types at once.
Skipping fieldset legends. Sighted users infer groups from spacing, but screen-reader users hear fields without context — the legend is announced with each control inside the group.
Validating only the fun fields. Decide required/pattern from the business rules first — what the process genuinely needs — not from which attributes are easy to add.
lessons.proTip: Before writing any markup for a real form, list every field in a plain table with four columns: name, control type, required or optional, validation rule. Ten minutes of that table saves an hour of restructuring — and the table converts almost line-by-line into HTML.

coding.intro: You will build the DevConf registration form the way a working developer would: plan the fields, group them, label them, validate them, then wire up submission.

sections.heading: Step 1 — from requirements to a field list
sections.body:
Every good form starts as a list, not as markup. Read the requirement — 'collect attendee details, ticket type, optional workshops, session preference, arrival date and dietary needs' — and translate each noun into a field with a control type chosen by the shape of its answer.

Free short text with a known format? An input with the most specific type available: text for the name, email for the address, tel for the phone. Exactly one choice from a small visible set? Radio buttons — the ticket type. Any number of choices? Checkboxes — the workshops. One choice from a long list? A select, with optgroups once the list needs organising — the session preference. A calendar value? A date input. Free-form prose? A textarea — the dietary notes.

This mapping is the highest-leverage decision in form design: choosing radios where checkboxes belong changes what data can exist, and choosing text where date belongs throws away the browser's picker, keyboard and validation for free.

sections.heading: Step 2 — grouping with fieldset and legend
sections.body:
A flat run of twelve controls reads as a wall. The fieldset element draws related controls into one group, and its first child, legend, names the group. Browsers render a light border with the legend set into it — instantly scannable structure with zero CSS.

Group by topic as the user thinks of it: who I am (name, email, phone), what I am buying (ticket type), what I want to attend (workshops, session). Radio groups almost always deserve their own fieldset, because the legend asks the question — 'Ticket type' — and the radio labels answer it: Standard, Student, Speaker.

The accessibility payoff is concrete: when a screen-reader user lands on a radio labelled 'Student', the legend is announced with it — 'Ticket type, Student' — restoring the context that sighted users get from proximity. A fieldset can also be disabled as a unit, switching off a whole section while its data stays visible.
sections.code:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Ticket type</legend>
  <input type="radio" id="t-std" name="ticket" value="standard" checked>
  <label for="t-std">Standard</label>
  <input type="radio" id="t-stu" name="ticket" value="student">
  <label for="t-stu">Student</label>
  <input type="radio" id="t-spk" name="ticket" value="speaker">
  <label for="t-spk">Speaker</label>
</fieldset>

sections.heading: Step 3 — labels on every control, no exceptions
sections.body:
Every control gets a label element tied to it by for on the label matching the id on the control. The binding does three jobs at once: screen readers announce the label when the field gains focus, clicking the label focuses or toggles the control (a big target win for checkboxes and radios on touch screens), and the association survives any CSS repositioning.

Convention differs by control shape: for text-like inputs, selects and textareas the label sits before the control; for each radio and checkbox it sits after its box. Placeholders, as always, are format hints inside the box — never a substitute for the label naming the field.

Remember the parallel naming system: id serves labels and fragment links and must be unique; name serves submission and repeats across a radio group on purpose. The ticket radios share name="ticket" — that shared name is what makes them mutually exclusive — while each keeps a unique id for its own label.
sections.code:
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" required autocomplete="email">

<input type="checkbox" id="w-a11y" name="workshops" value="a11y">
<label for="w-a11y">Accessibility deep-dive</label>

sections.heading: Step 4 — the long list: select with optgroups
sections.body:
The session preference has nine options across three time blocks — too many for radios, which excel up to about five visible choices. A select compresses the list into one control, and optgroup elements with label attributes split it into Morning, Afternoon and Evening blocks the user can scan.

Give each option a stable machine value distinct from its display text, so the talk can be renamed without breaking the backend. Lead with a 'please choose' option holding an empty value; combined with required on the select, it forces a real selection while giving the closed control an honest initial state.

The workshops question next to it is the deliberate contrast: it allows zero, one or many selections, so it is checkboxes sharing a name — never a multiple select, whose Ctrl-click convention loses data to every user who does not know it.
sections.code:
<label for="session">Preferred session</label>
<select id="session" name="session" required>
  <option value="">-- Choose a session --</option>
  <optgroup label="Morning">
    <option value="html-forms">Forms in depth</option>
    <option value="css-grid">Grid layouts</option>
  </optgroup>
  <optgroup label="Afternoon">
    <option value="a11y">Accessibility clinic</option>
    <option value="perf">Performance tuning</option>
  </optgroup>
</select>

sections.heading: Step 5 — the validation layer
sections.body:
Validation is a layer you apply after the structure works, and it starts from business rules: registration is impossible without a name and a reachable email, so those two are required. The phone is optional — but if present it must look like a phone number, so it gets a pattern like [0-9 +-]{7,15} and, inseparably, a title spelling out the format for the error bubble.

The date input can encode the event window: min and max bound arrival to the conference dates, and the browser's picker greys out everything else. The email field validates its shape by type alone. Radios with a checked default cannot be submitted empty; checkboxes are genuinely optional, so they carry no constraints at all.

And the rule that has ended careers when forgotten: everything re-validates on the server. Browser validation is the courtesy layer that catches typos in milliseconds; the server is the enforcement layer that attackers cannot switch off. Both check the same rules, stated once in your field-planning table.
sections.code:
<input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
<input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone"
       pattern="[0-9 +-]{7,15}"
       title="7 to 15 digits, spaces, + or - allowed">
<input type="date" id="arrival" name="arrival"
       min="2026-09-14" max="2026-09-16">

sections.heading: Step 6 — submission: method, action and the button
sections.body:
The form element's action names the URL that processes the data and method chooses the HTTP verb. Registrations are method="post" without debate: the submission changes server state, and it carries personal data that must not appear in URLs, browser history, server logs or shared links — all places GET query strings end up. GET is for safe, repeatable reads like searches; POST is for everything that creates or changes.

Close the form with an explicit <button type="submit">. The explicit type is a discipline from earlier lessons — any typeless button inside a form is a submit button in disguise — and the button element leaves room for richer content than an input ever could.

Before calling a form finished, run the submission checklist: does every control have a name (unnamed controls silently vanish from the data)? Do the radios share exactly one name? Does the empty-value placeholder option pair with required? Does keyboard-only Tab-and-Space operation reach everything? Five questions, and every one of them is a bug you now know how to prevent.

tasks.errorMessage: Expected three radio buttons all named "ticket" — different names would allow multiple ticket types at once.

tasks.instruction: Add two workshop checkboxes (name="workshops") and a session select containing two optgroups (Morning, Afternoon) with options inside.
tasks.hint: Checkboxes for any-number choices; <optgroup label="Morning"> groups the long select list.
tasks.errorMessage: The session select needs at least two <optgroup> elements — and do not forget the workshop checkboxes.

tasks.instruction: Add a labelled arrival date input (type="date", name="arrival") and a labelled dietary-notes textarea (name="diet").
tasks.hint: The date type gives you the native picker; the textarea takes rows and cols for its initial size.
tasks.errorMessage: No date input found — arrival needs <input type="date"> with a label (plus the dietary textarea).

tasks.instruction: Apply the validation layer: required on name and email, and on the phone input a pattern of [0-9 +-]{7,15} with a title explaining it.
tasks.hint: Pattern and title travel together — the title text appears in the browser's error bubble.
tasks.errorMessage: The tel input needs both a pattern and a title (and name/email should be required).
